summary: In large RTP sessions using RTCP feedback, many receivers sending feedback at once can overload a feedback target. This RFC defines an RTCP extension for third-party loss reports, for cases where feedback should not be forwarded to every receiver.

eli5.summary: In a huge class, if everyone yells that they missed a word, the teacher is swamped. This lets one person report for others.

questions: what is rtcp third-party loss report
how to avoid feedback overload in rtp sessions
what is a nack storm in rtp
how does rtcp feedback suppression work
subtitle: Lets a middlebox tell RTP receivers that a loss is already known, so they stop piling feedback onto the sender.

tldr.problem: In a large RTP session, a loss event can make many receivers send the same feedback (NACK, FIR, PLI) at once, overloading the media source or feedback target and the network.
tldr.mechanism: An intermediary that has already heard about the loss sends a Third-Party Loss Report (TPLR) in two forms: a transport-layer one (FMT=7) and a payload-specific one (FMT=8). Receivers that understand it hold back their own feedback for those packets.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that adds two RTCP feedback messages and two SDP parameters, tllei and pslei. Suppression is best effort, because nodes that do not understand the message ignore it.

today: RFC 6642 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2012. The unit metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: The Feedback Storm Problem
sections.content:
RTCP feedback messages from RFC 4585 let receivers in an RTP session report events and ask the media source (or a delegated feedback target) to act. When many receivers send the same or equivalent message at once, the source, the network or both can suffer transient overload. The RFC calls this a feedback storm or NACK storm.

One example is video in a multipoint switching conference. When the speaker changes, many receivers may lose synchronization at the same moment and each sends a Full Intra Request (FIR, from RFC 5104) blind, without knowing others have done the same.

Normally the storm is avoided by forwarding feedback to all receivers so they can suppress duplicates. This RFC covers cases where that forwarding is not recommended, and defines a message that says explicitly that feedback for a given loss is not needed.
sections.eli5: If a hundred kids all raise their hands to say the same thing, the teacher cannot cope. This is a way to tell everyone 'the teacher already knows.'

sections.title: Where the Report Is Used
sections.content:
The RFC describes five situations where an intermediary may send a TPLR.

  • Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) with unicast feedback (RFC 5760): in the Distribution Source Feedback Summary Model, the distribution source may not redistribute a NACK, for example to avoid revealing who sent it. It can send a TPLR to receivers that would not otherwise see the NACK.
  • Rapid acquisition of multicast streams (RFC 6285): a Burst/Retransmission Source may send a NACK or TPLR to the distribution source.
  • Transport translator (RFC 5117): it may forward a TPLR like other RTCP traffic.
  • Multipoint Control Unit: when it starts to receive FIRs, it can suppress the other participants by sending a TPLR.
  • Mixer: it may send a FIR or PLI towards the media source on behalf of all participants and send a TPLR to those expected to send one.
sections.eli5: Anyone standing in the middle, like a class monitor, can tell the others 'I have already told the teacher.'

sections.title: How the Report Behaves
sections.content:
The TPLR tells a receiver that the sender of the message has received reports that the indicated packets were lost, and asks it not to send feedback about them. This differs from a NACK, which says the sender itself saw the loss. The intermediary generating a TPLR may not have seen the loss at all. A TPLR has no retransmission request semantics.

It follows the same timing rule as a NACK from RFC 4585 and may go in a regular compound RTCP packet or an early RTCP packet. Intermediaries that receive a TPLR MUST NOT send their own TPLR for the same sequence numbers and SHOULD forward the one from upstream. They may send a TPLR for different losses they see.

A receiver that gets a TPLR MUST follow the NACK suppression rules of RFC 4585 and refrain from sending a NACK or FIR for the reported packets. A TPLR may be retransmitted for robustness; the receiver treats a repeat like the first. Feedback already sent before the TPLR arrived is not undone, and nodes that do not understand the message may still send feedback, so the sender cannot be certain it reduces feedback.
sections.eli5: Hearing 'we already know,' you stay quiet. If someone did not hear the announcement, they may still shout, so it only helps most of the time.

sections.title: The Two Feedback Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines two RTCP feedback messages that use the common header from Section 6.1 of RFC 4585.

The transport-layer message uses packet type RTPFB with FMT=7. Its feedback control information holds one or more TLLEI entries, each with a 16-bit Packet ID (PID, the RTP sequence number of a lost packet) and a 16-bit bitmask (BLP) covering the 16 packets after it, defined as in RFC 4585. All entries apply to the media source in the header. The length field MUST be N+2 for N entries.

The payload-specific message uses PSFB with FMT=8 and is meant to suppress FIR and PLI. The header's media source SSRC is not used and SHALL be 0. Each entry (PSLEI) is a single 32-bit SSRC of a media source, and the length field MUST again be N+2.
sections.eli5: There are two note forms. One lists exactly which numbered pages were lost. The other just names whose video needs a fresh picture.

sections.title: SDP Signaling
sections.content: Support is negotiated with the rtcp-fb attribute from Section 4 of RFC 4585. The RFC adds two parameters to nack: tllei for Transport-Layer Third-Party Loss Early Indication and pslei for Payload-Specific Third-Party Loss Early Indication. The ABNF extends rtcp-fb-val with "nack" rtcp-fb-nack-param, keeping a generic alternative for future commands.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side says which special notes it understands, using two new labels.

sections.title: Security and Registrations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4585 also apply. A spoofed or malicious TPLR makes receivers hold back feedback, so missing packets are not repaired in a timely way, which hurts applications relying on timely retransmission. The suggested defence is authentication and integrity protection, for example with the SAVPF profile combining Secure RTP (RFC 3711) and AVPF (RFC 5124).

An intermediary that is not visible at the RTP layer can only send reports for the media source by spoofing its SSRC, which is difficult with SRTP. An intermediary visible at the RTP layer is fine if it is part of the session's security context.

IANA registered tllei and pslei in the SDP nack attribute values, FMT 7 (TLLEI) in the RTPFB registry and FMT 8 (PSLEI) in the PSFB registry.
sections.eli5: A fake 'we already know' announcement could make everyone stay quiet when help is needed, so the announcements should be signed.

fields.name: PID
fields.desc: RTP sequence number of a lost packet.

fields.name: BLP
fields.desc: Bitmask of the 16 RTP packets after PID that are also lost.
